items.c: The single most reliable sinus criterion is an upright P in II with an inverted P in aVR; check both before ever labelling a rhythm 'sinus'.
items.a: Normal Sinus Rhythm
items.cr: Surawicz B, Knilans TK. Chous Electrocardiography in Clinical Practice

items.c: Widespread ST depression maximal in V4-V6/I/II with ST elevation in aVR suggests left main or triple-vessel ischaemia — an NSTEMI that behaves like an emergency.
items.a: NSTEMI / Subendocardial Ischaemia
items.cr: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2018)

items.c: Reciprocal ST depression in aVL is the most sensitive early sign of inferior STEMI — it can appear before the inferior ST elevation is obvious.
items.a: Inferior STEMI (RCA)
items.cr: ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (and ACC/AHA/SCAI guidelines on coronary revascularization)

items.c: A regular narrow tachycardia at exactly ~150 bpm is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise — adenosine or carotid massage increases block and reveals the sawtooth waves.
items.a: Atrial flutter
items.cr: ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Patients With Supraventricular Tachycardia

items.c: De Winter T waves (upsloping ST depression with tall symmetric T at the J point in V1-V6) are a STEMI-equivalent of proximal LAD occlusion — activate the cath lab even without ST elevation.
items.a: Anterior STEMI (LAD Occlusion)
items.cr: Fourth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (ESC/ACC/AHA/WHF)

items.c: Look at V1: coarse fibrillatory waves can mimic flutter, but true AF never shows a constant, repeating atrial cycle length.
items.a: Atrial Fibrillation
items.cr: ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation

items.c: The block is in the AV node in the vast majority of cases, so atropine and vagolytic manoeuvres shorten the PR — a clue to nodal (versus infranodal) level of delay.
items.a: First-degree AV block
items.cr: ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay (2018)

items.t: Mobitz II (Second-Degree AV Block, Type II)
items.c: The PR before and after the dropped beat is identical — 'the PR that doesn't change' — and the P waves march right through the pause on time. A wide QRS strongly supports the infranodal Mobitz II diagnosis.
items.a: Mobitz II (Second-Degree AV Block, Type II)
items.rn: Mobitz II (Second-Degree AV Block, Type II)
items.cr: ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients with Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

items.c: The R-R interval actually SHORTENS before the dropped beat, because the biggest PR jump is between beats 1 and 2 — spotting the shortening R-R plus grouped beating clinches Wenckebach even before you measure every PR.
items.a: Mobitz I (Wenckebach) Second-Degree AV Block
items.cr: ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

items.c: The distinguishing rule is that in TRUE complete block the atrial rate is faster than the ventricular rate — the sinus node is trying to drive but nothing gets through, so the ventricles fall back on an escape focus.
items.a: Complete (Third-Degree) AV Block
items.cr: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

items.c: Look at V1 for the classic 'M' (rSR') and at I/V6 for the reciprocal broad slurred S — together they nail RBBB and distinguish it from LBBB.
items.a: Right bundle branch block
items.cr: ACC/AHA/HRS 2018 Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

items.c: In LBBB, remember 'WiLLiaM' — W-shape in V1 and M-shape in V6 (and 'MaRRoW' for RBBB).
items.a: Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB)
items.cr: ACC/AHA/HRS recommendations for the standardization and interpretation of the ECG (Surawicz et al., intraventricular conduction disturbances)

items.c: Compare the tachycardia ECG with the patient's sinus ECG — a new terminal 'r' in V1 or 's' in the inferior leads during tachycardia is the buried retrograde P of typical AVNRT.
items.a: AVNRT (Atrioventricular Nodal Reentrant Tachycardia)
items.cr: 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Adult Patients With Supraventricular Tachycardia

items.c: Fusion and capture beats are pathognomonic of AV dissociation and effectively clinch VT; a concordant precordium or extreme (northwest) axis also strongly favours VT.
items.a: Monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
items.cr: ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for Management of Patients with Ventricular Arrhythmias and the Prevention of Sudden Cardiac Death

items.c: Measure QT in lead II or V5, use the tangent method to define T-wave end, and correct for rate; a QT that fails to shorten appropriately after exercise (prolonged QT in recovery) is a strong clue in borderline cases.
items.a: Long QT Syndrome
items.cr: ACC/AHA/HRS guidelines on ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death

items.c: IV calcium buys time but does NOT lower potassium — always follow it with shifting and elimination therapy, and recheck the level.
items.a: Hyperkalemia
items.cr: ACC/AHA/HRS and ACLS resources on management of life-threatening electrolyte abnormalities

items.c: A notch or slur on the down-stroke of the R wave (the J wave) with concave ST elevation and a stable serial ECG points to early repolarisation rather than infarction.
items.a: Early repolarization

items.c: If the P waves are all identical sinus P's and the PR is fixed but the R-R gently waxes and wanes with breathing, it is sinus arrhythmia, not a pathological irregular rhythm.
items.a: Sinus arrhythmia

items.c: One consistent but abnormally shaped P (e.g. inverted in II with a short PR) before every QRS = single ectopic atrial focus; the consistency is what separates it from wandering pacemaker.
items.a: Ectopic atrial rhythm

items.c: Three or more P-wave shapes with a changing PR at a rate under 100 defines wandering pacemaker; the only step from here to MAT is the rate crossing 100 bpm.
items.a: Wandering atrial pacemaker

items.c: Sinus bradycardia + high QRS voltage + early repolarisation + vagal first-degree AV block that all normalise with exercise is the classic benign athlete pattern.
items.a: Athlete's heart pattern

items.c: Inverted P-QRS-T in lead I with an upright aVR and R waves that shrink across the precordium is dextrocardia, not lateral infarction; repeat with reversed limb leads to confirm.
items.a: Dextrocardia

items.c: An upright P in lead II with a normal, constant PR before every QRS confirms sinus origin - the ONLY abnormality is the slow rate.
items.a: Sinus bradycardia

items.c: Measure the pause against the baseline P-P: if it is NOT a whole-number multiple, it is sinus arrest (failure of impulse formation) rather than SA exit block.
items.a: Sinus pause / arrest

items.c: The signature of type II SA exit block is a pause that is precisely double (an exact multiple of) the baseline P-P interval - the sinus node kept time even though a beat never made it out.
items.a: SA exit block

items.c: A regular, slow, NARROW-complex rhythm at 40-60 bpm with inverted P waves in lead II (before, in, or after the QRS) is a junctional escape - the AV junction is doing its job as a backup pacemaker.
items.a: Junctional escape rhythm

items.c: A slow (20-40 bpm), regular, WIDE-complex rhythm with P waves marching independently is a ventricular escape - the ventricle's fail-safe pacemaker in complete heart block. Pace, do not suppress.
items.a: Ventricular escape rhythm

items.c: The classic and dangerous signature is a long sinus pause immediately AFTER spontaneous termination of atrial fibrillation (tachy-brady syndrome) - this post-conversion pause is a common cause of syncope.
items.a: Sick sinus syndrome

items.c: QRS alternans and a retrograde P landing in the T wave (short-RP, RP<PR) during a very fast regular narrow SVT point to orthodromic AVRT over AVNRT.
items.a: Orthodromic AVRT

items.c: Adenosine that causes transient AV block yet lets the abnormal P waves march on unchanged confirms atrial tachycardia rather than AV-node-dependent re-entry.
items.a: Focal atrial tachycardia

items.c: Three or more clearly different P-wave shapes with varying PR intervals in one lead, at a rate over 100, is MAT — the presence of organised P waves is what separates it from AF.
items.a: Multifocal atrial tachycardia

items.c: Gradual warm-up/cool-down and an upright P before every QRS that matches the patient's baseline sinus P morphology distinguish sinus tachycardia from paroxysmal SVT.
items.a: Sinus tachycardia

items.c: A regular narrow tachycardia with inverted inferior P waves that does NOT break with adenosine points to an automatic junctional focus rather than re-entrant AVNRT.
items.a: Junctional tachycardia

items.c: Give IV magnesium first regardless of the serum level, and remember torsades is pause-dependent — raising the heart rate (isoprenaline or pacing) shortens the QT and suppresses it.
items.a: Torsades de pointes

items.c: Coarse VF is more likely to respond to defibrillation and generally reflects a shorter arrest time than fine VF — but both are shockable, so shock early.
items.a: Ventricular fibrillation

items.c: In a young patient with a wide, regular tachycardia and a known delta wave on prior ECGs, think antidromic AVRT — but treat any diagnostic uncertainty as VT and give procainamide, not AV-nodal blockers.
items.a: Antidromic AVRT

items.c: Rate is the key discriminator: a wide, regular rhythm at 40-120 bpm is AIVR, whereas the same morphology at >120 bpm is VT — and AIVR after PCI is a welcome sign of reperfusion.
items.a: Accelerated idioventricular rhythm

items.c: The two single most useful discriminators are AV dissociation (with fusion/capture beats) and clinical context — a broad tachycardia in an older patient with prior MI is VT until proven otherwise.
items.a: VT vs SVT with aberrancy

items.c: The give-away is a run of two or more blocked P's WITH at least one conducted beat carrying a constant PR — that single conducted beat proves it is high-grade block and not complete heart block.
items.a: High-grade AV block

items.c: Ask 'who is faster?': if the ventricles are keeping up with or beating faster than the atria, it is dissociation by usurpation (benign) — not complete block, where the atria always outrun a slow escape.
items.a: AV dissociation

items.c: Think LAFB whenever you see marked left axis deviation with a NARROW QRS and qR in aVL / rS in the inferior leads.
items.a: Left anterior fascicular block

items.c: LPFB is the mirror image of LAFB: right axis with qR inferiorly and rS in I/aVL, QRS still narrow.
items.a: Left posterior fascicular block

items.c: RBBB + left axis deviation = RBBB + LAFB, the classic and commonest bifascicular block; RBBB + right axis = RBBB + LPFB.
items.a: Bifascicular block

items.c: The most reliable ECG sign of genuine trifascicular disease is ALTERNATING bundle branch block, not merely a long PR added to bifascicular block.
items.a: Trifascicular block

items.c: If the QRS is wide but the morphology is neither the RBBB 'M in V1' nor the LBBB 'M in V6', call it a nonspecific IVCD and go hunting for the cause.
items.a: Nonspecific intraventricular conduction delay

items.c: Isolated ST elevation in aVL with reciprocal depression in lead III is the 'South African flag' pattern of a high first-diagonal occlusion — easy to overlook.
items.a: Lateral STEMI

items.c: Flip the ECG upside-down and hold it to the light: the V1-V3 changes become recognizable ST elevation and Q waves of a posterior STEMI.
items.a: Posterior MI

items.c: In inferior STEMI, ST elevation in V1 that is greater in V1 than the depression in V2, or any ST elevation in V4R, points to concurrent RV infarction.
items.a: Right-ventricular infarction

items.c: Type A Wellens shows biphasic (up-then-down) T waves in V2-V3; Type B shows deep symmetric inversion — both mean the same critical proximal LAD lesion.
items.a: Wellens syndrome

items.c: The de Winter pattern is often static rather than evolving — if you wait for it to become a textbook STEMI you may be waiting through a completed anterior infarct.
items.a: De Winter T-waves

items.c: Hyperacute T waves are 'fatter' — the increased area under the T wave and broad base distinguish them from the narrow, tented, symmetric T of hyperkalemia.
items.a: Hyperacute T-waves

items.c: A QS complex in V1-V3 with poor R-wave progression is the classic signature of an old anteroseptal infarct.
items.a: Old MI / pathologic Q-waves

items.c: aVR ST elevation that is greater than the ST elevation in V1, combined with widespread ST depression, points to left main rather than isolated LAD disease.
items.a: Left main / aVR ST-elevation

items.c: The ratio of ST elevation to T-wave height in lead V6 (>0.25 favors pericarditis) and PR depression help separate pericarditis from early repolarization/STEMI.
items.a: Pericarditis vs STEMI

items.c: Cornell and Sokolow-Lyon are highly specific but poorly sensitive; a normal ECG does not exclude LVH, so echo remains the reference standard for LV mass.
items.a: Left ventricular hypertrophy

items.c: A dominant R in V1 plus right axis deviation and a peaked P in lead II (P pulmonale) is the classic RVH triad, most often seen in chronic pulmonary hypertension.
items.a: Right ventricular hypertrophy

items.c: The single most reliable ECG sign of LAE is the Morris index in V1: a terminal negative P deflection at least one small square wide and one small square deep.
items.a: Left atrial enlargement

items.c: RAE increases P amplitude, not duration - a tall peaked P >= 2.5 mm in II with a normal-width P wave is the signature, classically 'P pulmonale' in COPD.
items.a: Right atrial enlargement

items.c: Suspect biventricular hypertrophy when you see LVH voltage but the axis is right, not left - opposing hypertrophy vectors cancel, so 'contradictory' findings are the tell.
items.a: Biventricular hypertrophy

items.c: You cannot correct refractory hypokalemia without also correcting magnesium — always check and replace Mg.
items.a: Hypokalemia

items.c: A visibly short ST segment with the T wave 'hugging' the QRS should prompt an immediate ionized calcium check.
items.a: Hypercalcemia

items.c: Hypocalcemia lengthens the ST segment (not the T wave) — a long isoelectric ST with a normal T is the giveaway.
items.a: Hypocalcemia

items.c: Osborn wave size tracks inversely with core temperature — bigger J waves mean colder patient.
items.a: Hypothermia (Osborn waves)

items.c: IV magnesium is the treatment of choice for torsades de pointes even when the serum magnesium is normal.
items.a: Hypomagnesemia

items.c: The scooped 'Salvador Dali moustache' ST depression with a SHORT QT is the fingerprint of digoxin effect - ischaemia and hypokalaemia both prolong, not shorten, the QT.
items.a: Digoxin effect

items.c: Digoxin toxicity can cause almost any arrhythmia EXCEPT a fast, well-conducted SVT - the pairing of increased automaticity with blocked conduction (e.g. atrial tachycardia WITH AV block, or a regularized slow ventricular rate in AF) is the giveaway.
items.a: Digoxin toxicity

items.c: The QRS duration is the single best bedside prognostic tool: >100 ms predicts seizures and >160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmias - a tall terminal R in aVR confirms the sodium-channel-blocking mechanism.
items.a: TCA overdose

items.c: If the standard V1–V2 look non-diagnostic but suspicion is high, move V1–V2 up to the 2nd/3rd intercostal space — this frequently unmasks the coved type 1 pattern because the RVOT substrate sits high.
items.a: Brugada syndrome

items.c: A QT that looks 'too short' with tall pointed T waves that begin almost immediately after the QRS — and does not lengthen at slow rates — should prompt QTc calculation and consideration of SQTS rather than being dismissed as normal.
items.a: Short QT syndrome

items.c: A completely normal resting ECG does NOT exclude CPVT — order an exercise (treadmill) test in any young patient with exertional or emotion-triggered syncope; the diagnostic bidirectional VT appears only with catecholamine load.
items.a: CPVT

items.c: A negative delta wave can create a pseudo-infarct Q-wave pattern — always inspect the PR and QRS onset before diagnosing an old MI, and read the delta-wave polarity across leads to localize the pathway.
items.a: WPW (pre-excitation)

items.c: The epsilon wave is subtle — look for a small reproducible deflection just after the QRS in V1–V3, use high-gain/right-sided leads or the Fontaine bipolar leads, and pair it with the terminal activation duration to strengthen the diagnosis.
items.a: ARVC / epsilon wave

items.c: Expected paced morphology is LBBB-like with left/superior axis; a paced QRS that turns predominantly positive in V1 (RBBB-like) should raise concern for lead perforation into the LV or coronary sinus.
items.a: Single-chamber paced rhythm

items.c: Count the spikes: two spikes per beat = dual-chamber (DDD) fully paced; a single spike before a wide QRS with a preceding sensed native P is atrial-sensed/ventricular-paced tracking.
items.a: Dual-chamber paced rhythm

items.c: New failure to capture with peaked T waves and a widened intrinsic QRS should prompt an immediate potassium check - hyperkalaemia raises the myocardial capture threshold.
items.a: Pacemaker failure to capture

items.c: Oversensing = a pause with NO spike (device wrongly thinks a beat occurred); a magnet restores pacing by switching to asynchronous mode, which is both diagnostic and a temporising treatment.
items.a: Pacemaker oversensing

items.c: Effective LV capture in CRT reverses the usual paced pattern: expect a dominant R wave in V1 and a negative QRS in lead I - the opposite of RV-only pacing.
items.a: Biventricular (CRT) pacing

items.c: PR-segment depression with reciprocal PR elevation in aVR is the earliest and most specific ECG sign, often preceding the classic ST changes.
items.a: Acute pericarditis

items.c: The classic tamponade triad on ECG is sinus tachycardia + low voltage + electrical alternans; total electrical alternans (P, QRS, and T all swinging) is the most specific sign.
items.a: Pericardial effusion (electrical alternans)

items.c: Simultaneous T-wave inversion in the anterior (V1-V3) AND inferior (III, aVF) leads is the most specific ECG sign of acute RV strain in PE and correlates with clot burden.
items.a: Pulmonary embolism (S1Q3T3)

items.c: A postmenopausal woman after an emotional stressor with "anterior STEMI" ECG, only modest troponin, and later deep diffuse TWI with a very long QT should raise Takotsubo.
items.a: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy

items.c: Deep, NARROW (dagger-like) septal Q waves in the lateral and inferior leads distinguish HCM from the broad Q waves of prior infarction; giant precordial T inversions suggest the apical (Yamaguchi) variant.
items.a: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

items.c: aVR with an upright, normal-looking P-QRS-T is the fastest tell for LA/RA reversal; a real aVR is almost always net negative. Always confirm normal precordial progression to separate it from dextrocardia.
items.a: Limb-lead misplacement

items.c: March out the R-R intervals across the noise: if they stay regular and QRS morphology is unchanged, the baseline chaos is artifact, not arrhythmia.
items.a: Tremor / muscle artifact

items.c: Count the artifact frequency: a beautifully regular buzz at ~50 or 60 Hz (far faster than any cardiac activity) is diagnostic of mains interference, not arrhythmia.
items.a: AC (mains) interference

items.c: Because the whole complex moves together and QRS shape is unchanged, re-measure ST segments relative to a stable PR baseline before ever calling ischaemia on a wandering tracing.
items.a: Motion / baseline wander

items.c: In true flutter the QRS is tethered to the flutter waves in a fixed ratio; in pseudo-flutter the sinus QRS marches independently and real P waves peek out when the tremor stops.
items.a: Pseudo-flutter (tremor)

items.c: The modified Smith criterion (discordant ST elevation ≥ 25% of the preceding S-wave depth) is more sensitive than the original absolute 5 mm discordance rule.
items.a: Sgarbossa criteria (MI in LBBB/paced)

items.c: A T-wave amplitude to QRS amplitude ratio <0.36 across the precordial leads favors LV aneurysm over acute anterior STEMI.
items.a: LV aneurysm (persistent ST elevation)

items.c: Reciprocal ST depression in aVL can be the earliest and most sensitive sign of an inferior STEMI, sometimes preceding the inferior ST elevation.
items.a: Reciprocal ST changes

items.c: The LVH strain T inversion is asymmetric ('hockey stick') with a gentle downslope and rapid upstroke, and is discordant to the tall R wave - unlike the deep symmetric inversions of ischaemia.
items.a: LVH with strain pattern

items.c: Shallow, asymmetric T-wave inversions confined to V1-V3 in a young, asymptomatic patient with an otherwise normal ECG are the benign juvenile pattern.
items.a: Juvenile T-wave pattern

items.c: A regular wide-complex tachycardia at exactly the programmed upper tracking rate in a dual-chamber pacemaker patient is PMT until proven otherwise - a magnet is both the immediate treatment and the diagnostic test.
items.a: Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia

items.c: You cannot label a strict 2:1 block as Mobitz I or II because you never see two conducted beats in a row — use the QRS width and PR instead, and try vagal manoeuvres vs atropine to shift the ratio and unmask the level.
items.a: 2:1 AV block

items.c: The way an SVT responds to adenosine is itself diagnostic: abrupt termination = AV-node-dependent re-entry (AVNRT/AVRT); transient block that exposes ongoing atrial activity = flutter or atrial tachycardia.
items.a: SVT response to adenosine

items.t: A Subtle Sign of Something Sinister
items.c: Inverted U waves are a subtle but specific sign of myocardial ischaemia and should not be dismissed as a normal variant.
items.a: A Subtle Sign of Something Sinister
items.rn: A Subtle Sign of Something Sinister

items.c: Retrograde P waves are inverted in the inferior leads and upright in aVR and V1, the opposite of normal sinus P wave polarity.
items.a: Accelerated Junctional Rhythm (AJR)

items.c: ST elevation in aVR with widespread ST depression is a marker of severe proximal / left main coronary disease and warrants urgent cardiology involvement.
items.a: Another Widow Maker

items.c: Anterior MI usually reflects LAD occlusion and carries the poorest prognosis, with higher in-hospital mortality, heart failure and lower ejection fraction than inferior MI.
items.a: Anterior Myocardial Infarction

items.c: Giant precordial T-wave inversion should prompt consideration of apical HCM, particularly in patients of Japanese ethnicity (Yamaguchi syndrome).
items.a: Apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (AHC)

items.c: A long-short R-R sequence terminating in a wide RBBB-type complex during AF suggests benign Ashman aberrancy rather than ventricular ectopy.
items.a: Ashman Phenomenon

items.c: Aslanger pattern flags an inferior OMI with concurrent multivessel disease; up to 13.3% of inferior MIs may present this way and be denied emergent revascularisation.
items.a: Aslanger Pattern: Another OMI?

items.c: In pre-excited AF the axis stays stable while QRS morphology varies subtly beat-to-beat, helping distinguish it from polymorphic VT.
items.a: Atrial fibrillation/flutter in pre-excitation

items.c: Antidromic AVRT is a regular wide-complex tachycardia that can be very difficult to distinguish from VT.
items.a: Atrioventricular Re-entry Tachycardia (AVRT)

items.t: AV Block: 2nd degree, Mobitz II (Hay block)
items.c: Mobitz II reflects His-Purkinje disease that tends to fail suddenly, so it is more likely to progress to complete heart block than Mobitz I.
items.a: AV Block: 2nd degree, Mobitz II (Hay block)
items.rn: AV Block: 2nd degree, Mobitz II (Hay block)

items.c: In 2:1 block you cannot see progressive PR changes, so QRS width and other clues are used to infer whether the mechanism is Mobitz I or II.
items.a: AV block: 2nd degree, “fixed ratio” blocks

items.c: The persistence of some conducted P waves distinguishes high grade AV block from complete heart block, where none conduct.
items.a: AV block: 2nd degree, “high-grade” AV block

items.c: In complete heart block the atrial and ventricular rates are entirely independent, with the atrial rate faster than the escape rate.
items.a: AV block: 3rd degree (complete heart block)

items.c: An ST-elevation-to-T-wave ratio < 0.25 in V6 and the absence of reciprocal ST depression favour BER over occlusion MI.
items.a: Benign Early Repolarisation

items.c: Propranolol behaves like a sodium-channel blocker in overdose, causing QRS widening and a positive R prime in aVR, unlike other beta-blockers.
items.a: Beta-blocker and Calcium-channel blocker toxicity

items.c: Diagnosis requires meeting both LAE and RAE criteria simultaneously, best assessed in leads II and V1.
items.a: Biatrial Enlargement

items.c: Unlike Brugada and LQTS, the ST depression of Bundgaard syndrome is stable over time and only accentuated by exercise.
items.a: Bundgaard syndrome

items.c: Cardiotoxicity is associated with massive ingestion (over 50 mg/kg); ECG changes are generally less dramatic than in TCA overdose.
items.a: Carbamazepine Cardiotoxicity

items.c: A ventricular ectopic landing on the preceding T wave (R-on-T), especially with a long QT, can trigger polymorphic VT / torsades and cardiac arrest.
items.a: Cardiac Megacode

items.c: Pre-excitation via the accessory pathway produces the slurred delta wave, short PR and broad QRS of WPW.
items.a: Delta Wave

items.c: Analysing the P-P interval pattern, not just the PR interval, is key to unmasking a concurrent SA nodal Wenckebach.
items.a: Diagnosis, Wenckebach Squared?

items.c: There are no ECG features unique to DCM, but a completely normal ECG makes the diagnosis less likely.
items.a: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM)

items.c: The quadrant method using leads I and aVF gives a rapid estimate of the QRS axis.
items.a: ECG Axis Interpretation

items.c: Right precordial T-wave inversion (RV strain) in the context of PE is associated with high pulmonary artery pressures.
items.a: ECG changes in Pulmonary Embolism

items.t: ECG in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
items.c: Hyperinflation causes clockwise rotation and a vertical heart, shifting the QRS axis rightward with poor precordial R-wave progression.
items.a: ECG in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
items.rn: ECG in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease

items.c: New RBBB with right ventricular strain in a dyspnoeic, shocked patient should raise strong suspicion of massive pulmonary embolism.
items.a: Electrocardiographic Exigency

items.c: Isolated first degree AV block is generally benign, but consider vagal tone, drugs, inferior MI, myocarditis and hyperkalaemia as causes.
items.a: First Degree Heart Block

items.c: A strikingly short QT interval with a family history of AF and sudden death should raise short QT syndrome, an inherited channelopathy.
items.a: Flummoxing Familial Fibrillation

items.c: Fusion (and capture) beats within a broad-complex tachycardia strongly support ventricular tachycardia over SVT with aberrancy.
items.a: Fusion Beats - Dressler beat

items.c: QT shortening is the hallmark of hypercalcaemia; Osborn waves appear only when calcium is severely elevated.
items.a: Hypercalcaemia ECG changes

items.c: In any patient with a bradycardic PEA arrest, suspect and empirically treat hyperkalaemia.
items.a: Hyperkalaemia ECG changes

items.c: New atrial fibrillation, especially with a rapid response, warrants checking thyroid function, as thyrotoxicosis is a reversible cause.
items.a: Hyperthyroidism ECG changes

items.c: The prominent U wave and long QU interval, not a truly prolonged QT, characterise significant hypokalaemia.
items.a: Hypokalaemia ECG changes

items.c: The Osborn (J) wave, a positive deflection at the J point, is the classic hypothermia finding, and its size tends to increase as temperature falls.
items.a: Hypothermia ECG changes

items.c: The triad of bradycardia, low voltage and diffuse T-wave inversion should prompt consideration of myxoedema.
items.a: Hypothyroidism ECG changes

items.c: This VT is verapamil-sensitive, making it a notable exception to the rule that calcium-channel blockers are dangerous in VT.
items.a: Idiopathic Fascicular Left Ventricular Tachycardia

items.c: Recording at half standard calibration (5 mm/mV) captures the full, overlapping Katz-Wachtel complexes without distortion.
items.a: Katz-Wachtel phenomenon

items.c: Complete inversion of lead I (P, QRS and T) with a positive aVR is a quick giveaway of LA/RA lead reversal.
items.a: Lead reversal: Left arm/right arm

items.c: In LAFB, depolarisation reaches the LV via the posterior fascicle first, directing the initial vector inferiorly then superolaterally, producing the qR/rS pattern and left axis deviation.
items.a: Left Anterior Fascicular Block (LAFB)

items.c: Normal axis lies between -30 and +90 degrees; pathological left axis deviation begins beyond -30 degrees.
items.a: Left Axis Deviation (LAD)

items.c: Appropriate discordance (ST segment and T wave deflect opposite to the dominant QRS) is expected in uncomplicated LBBB.
items.a: Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB)

items.c: In about 97% of cases the AV node is histologically normal; the lesion lies in both bundle branches.
items.a: Lenegre-Lev disease

items.c: Low voltage with tachycardia and electrical alternans mandates urgent assessment for tamponade.
items.a: Low QRS Voltage

items.c: Unlike WPW, the QRS is narrow with no delta wave because the accessory (James) fibres bypass only the AV node, not the His-Purkinje system.
items.a: Lown-Ganong-Levine syndrome

items.c: A small or absent S wave in lead I despite an RSR' in V1 is the tell-tale sign of standard MBBB.
items.a: Masquerading Bundle Branch Block (MBBB)

items.c: The prolonged QT of hypokalaemia is often an apparent QT caused by fusion of the T wave with a prominent U wave.
items.a: Metabolic Mayhem

items.c: A fully negative P wave in V1, or a biphasic/negative P in V2, should raise suspicion of high V1-V2 electrode placement.
items.a: Misplacement of V1 and V2

items.c: Dynamic ST-T changes during pain that resolve when the patient is pain-free strongly support ischaemia.
items.a: Myocardial Ischaemia

items.c: Myocarditis is frequently accompanied by pericarditis (myopericarditis), adding widespread concave ST elevation and PR changes.
items.a: Myocarditis ECG changes

items.c: About 25-30% of NSTEMI patients have a totally occluded artery; expert reading reclassifies many as OMI needing urgent reperfusion.
items.a: OMI: Replacing the STEMI misnomer

items.c: Osborn waves become more prominent as core temperature drops and often coexist with bradycardia and tremor (shivering) artefact.
items.a: Osborn Wave (J Wave)

items.c: Atrial abnormalities are best seen in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF) and V1, where P waves are most prominent.
items.a: P wave

items.c: Pacing spikes that fall within QRS complexes suggest undersensing of native cardiac activity.
items.a: Pacemaker Malfunction

items.c: In a paced patient an extremely wide QRS tachycardia should prompt consideration of metabolic causes and device behaviour, not only VT.
items.a: Pacemaker Panic #2

items.c: Right ventricular pacing produces an LBBB-pattern wide QRS with appropriate discordant ST-T changes, analogous to LBBB.
items.a: Pacemaker Rhythms - Normal Patterns

items.c: Rate-dependent (aberrant) LBBB narrows as the heart rate slows, distinguishing it from true VT.
items.a: Pain free and in VT?

items.c: PR depression with reciprocal PR elevation and ST depression in aVR is highly suggestive of pericarditis.
items.a: Pericarditis ECG Changes

items.t: Polymorphic VT and Torsades de Pointes (TdP)
items.c: Diagnosing torsades requires both polymorphic VT and QT prolongation; without a long QT it is simply polymorphic VT.
items.a: Polymorphic VT and Torsades de Pointes (TdP)
items.rn: Polymorphic VT and Torsades de Pointes (TdP)

items.c: Poor R wave progression is suggestive, not diagnostic; correlate with clinical context and prior ECGs.
items.a: Poor R Wave Progression (PRWP)

items.c: In AAI pacing the spikes precede P waves and the QRS stays narrow because normal AV conduction is preserved.
items.a: Post-op Pacing Puzzler

items.c: A delta wave with a short PR is the hallmark of ventricular pre-excitation via an accessory pathway.
items.a: Pre-excitation syndromes

items.c: Unlike a PVC, the pause after a PAC is not fully compensatory because the ectopic beat resets the sinus node.
items.a: Premature Atrial Complex (PAC)

items.c: A retrograde inverted P wave in the inferior leads adjacent to a narrow premature QRS suggests a junctional origin.
items.a: Premature Junctional Complex (PJC)

items.c: A full compensatory pause (the interval spanning the PVC equals two sinus cycles) helps distinguish a PVC from a PAC.
items.a: Premature Ventricular Complex (PVC)

items.c: In a young patient with pre-excitation, a regular broad complex tachycardia may be antidromic AVRT, in which the accessory pathway conducts antegradely.
items.a: Puzzling Paroxysmal Palpitations

items.c: Small narrow Q waves in the lateral leads are normal septal Q waves; depth and width define pathology.
items.a: Q Wave

items.c: A narrow QRS localises the origin to at or above the AV node (supraventricular).
items.a: QRS Interval

items.c: In acute poisoning, torsades risk is better described by the absolute QT with simultaneous heart rate plotted on the QT nomogram than by the QTc.
items.a: Quetiapine Toxicity

items.c: A prolonged R wave peak time in aVL is a supportive feature of left anterior fascicular block.
items.a: R Wave Peak Time RWPT

items.c: Deep, widespread cerebral T-wave inversions with QT prolongation are classic for subarachnoid haemorrhage.
items.a: Raised Intracranial Pressure ECG Changes

items.c: In isolated RBBB the initial septal and left ventricular activation is normal, so the cardiac axis stays normal.
items.a: Right Bundle Branch Block (RBBB)

items.c: An LBBB-morphology VT with an inferior axis in a structurally normal heart suggests RVOT tachycardia.
items.a: Right Ventricular Outflow Tract (RVOT) Tachycardia

items.c: Tachy-brady syndrome (sick sinus) alternates tachyarrhythmia with symptomatic bradycardia and pauses, and typically needs a permanent pacemaker.
items.a: Risky Rhythyms

items.c: Mobitz II is more likely to progress to complete heart block and usually warrants pacing, unlike the often-benign Mobitz I.
items.a: Second-degree Atrioventricular block

items.t: Seizures, Somnolence and a Scary ECG
items.c: A dominant terminal R wave in aVR with QRS widening after seizures and coma points to sodium-channel blocker (tricyclic) toxicity, treated with sodium bicarbonate.
items.a: Seizures, Somnolence and a Scary ECG
items.rn: Seizures, Somnolence and a Scary ECG

items.t: Shock, syncope and severe chest pain
items.c: Chest pain with shock, pulmonary oedema and ventricular arrhythmia signals a large territory at risk such as the left main or proximal LAD.
items.a: Shock, syncope and severe chest pain
items.rn: Shock, syncope and severe chest pain

items.c: Sick sinus syndrome is often due to idiopathic degenerative fibrosis; symptomatic cases usually require a permanent pacemaker.
items.a: Sinus Node Dysfunction (Sick Sinus Syndrome)

items.c: Epsilon waves and exertional VT in a young athlete point to arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy.
items.a: Sudden Syncope at Soccer

items.c: Paroxysmal SVT (AVNRT/AVRT) starts and stops abruptly and often responds to vagal manoeuvres or adenosine.
items.a: Supraventricular Tachycardia (SVT)

items.c: Electrical alternans with sinus tachycardia suggests a large pericardial effusion, with the heart swinging within the fluid.
items.a: The Paradoxical Alternative

items.c: Bidirectional VT with a beat-to-beat alternating axis is strongly associated with severe digoxin toxicity and CPVT.
items.a: Troubling Tachycardia

items.c: Ventricular flutter looks identical when the ECG is turned upside down, reflecting its symmetric sine-wave morphology.
items.a: Ventricular Flutter

items.c: AV dissociation with capture and fusion beats is highly specific for ventricular tachycardia.
items.a: Ventricular Tachycardia - Monomorphic VT

items.c: Algorithms such as Brugada and Vereckei help distinguish VT from SVT with aberrancy in a regular broad complex tachycardia.
items.a: VT or not VT

items.t: Who's Afraid Of The Big Bad Wolff?
items.c: An irregular, rapid, broad complex tachycardia with varying QRS width suggests pre-excited atrial fibrillation in WPW.
items.a: Who's Afraid Of The Big Bad Wolff?
items.rn: Who's Afraid Of The Big Bad Wolff?

items.c: de Winter T waves (upsloping ST depression with tall symmetric precordial T waves) are a STEMI-equivalent indicating proximal LAD occlusion.
items.a: Winter is Coming

items.c: A negative P wave and QRS in lead I with normal precordial R wave progression indicates left-right arm lead reversal rather than dextrocardia.
items.a: Case 2 - Limb lead reversal

items.t: Case 3 - Conservative management with nonsteroidal analgesia
items.c: Diffuse (non-territorial) ST elevation with PR displacement favours pericarditis over MI, which tends to be localised.
items.a: Case 3 - Conservative management with nonsteroidal analgesia
items.rn: Case 3 - Conservative management with nonsteroidal analgesia

items.c: Peaked tented T waves with flattening or loss of P waves and QRS widening indicate progressive hyperkalaemia requiring urgent treatment.
items.a: Case 4 - Hyperkalemia

items.t: Case 5 - Sinus rhythm with 2:1 AV block
items.c: In 2:1 AV block, a narrow QRS with a prolonged PR favours nodal block, while a wide QRS or a PR of 160 ms or less favours infranodal block.
items.a: Case 5 - Sinus rhythm with 2:1 AV block
items.rn: Case 5 - Sinus rhythm with 2:1 AV block

items.t: Case 6 - Ectopic atrial rhythm with variable AV block
items.c: A very long QT(U) interval in a patient on quinidine or another class 1A agent predisposes to torsades and can occur even at therapeutic levels.
items.a: Case 6 - Ectopic atrial rhythm with variable AV block
items.rn: Case 6 - Ectopic atrial rhythm with variable AV block

items.c: A systematic, beat-by-beat approach lets you decode a busy Holter strip that mixes several rhythms.
items.a: [blog] An Interesting Holter Strip

items.c: A retrograde P wave from a PVC can reset the sinus node, altering the timing of the next sinus beat.
items.a: [blog] INTERESTING HOLTER-STRIP

items.c: A retrograde P wave may fall before, within, or after the QRS depending on how deep the junctional focus is and its conduction timing.
items.a: [blog] Junctional Escape Rhythm, Very Slow

items.c: A perfectly regular narrow-complex bradycardia effectively excludes conducted atrial fibrillation, which is irregular.
items.a: [blog] JUNCTIONAL ESCAPE RHYTM

items.c: LBBB can appear without any known cardiac disease, as in this preoperative screening ECG.
items.a: [blog] LBBB

items.c: In LBBB the leftward leads (I, aVL, V5, V6) are upright while the rightward and anterior leads are deeply negative.
items.a: [blog] Left Bundle Branch Block

items.t: [blog] Long QT Syndrome,Look Closely and Do Not Trust the ECG-Computer
items.c: A broad, prominent T wave beginning right after the QRS can fool the computer into reporting a falsely short QT; always remeasure manually.
items.a: [blog] Long QT Syndrome,Look Closely and Do Not Trust the ECG-Computer
items.rn: [blog] Long QT Syndrome,Look Closely and Do Not Trust the ECG-Computer

items.c: Always hunt for a premature P wave hidden in the preceding T wave before diagnosing a pause as AV block.
items.a: [blog] NON-CONDUCTED PAC

items.c: Identical P-wave morphology across an irregular rhythm points to sinus arrhythmia rather than atrial ectopy.
items.a: [blog] Non-respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia

items.c: Compare T-wave shapes across beats; a subtle bump present on some T waves but absent on others reveals a hidden blocked PAC.
items.a: [blog] Nonconducted PACs

items.c: A fusion beat at the onset of a broad-complex run is strong evidence for a ventricular origin.
items.a: [blog] NONSUSTAINED VT

items.c: A fusion beat's morphology lies between a fully paced and a fully intrinsic complex, whereas a pseudofusion spike lands on an intrinsic beat without changing it.
items.a: [blog] PACEMAKER ECG: PSEUDOFUSION - FUSION

items.c: Finding a premature P wave (often best seen in V1) before a wide beat identifies aberrant supraventricular conduction rather than a ventricular ectopic.
items.a: [blog] PACS WITH ABERRANT CONDUCTION

items.c: Paroxysmal AF carries a particularly high embolic risk, so capturing even brief episodes justifies considering anticoagulation.
items.a: [blog] PAROXYSMAL ATRIAL FIBRILLATION

items.t: [blog] Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia during a stress EKG. What is the most likely cause?
items.c: Polymorphic VT with a normal baseline QT during exertion points to ischaemia rather than torsades de pointes.
items.a: [blog] Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia during a stress EKG. What is the most likely cause?
items.rn: [blog] Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia during a stress EKG. What is the most likely cause?

items.c: Torsades de pointes is only the correct label for polymorphic VT when the underlying rhythm shows a prolonged QT/QTc.
items.a: [blog] POLYMORPHIC VT

items.t: [blog] PVCs And Their Relationship to P waves, Some Examples
items.c: The position of surrounding P waves is a central clue for classifying a wide premature beat as ventricular or supraventricular.
items.a: [blog] PVCs And Their Relationship to P waves, Some Examples
items.rn: [blog] PVCs And Their Relationship to P waves, Some Examples

items.c: A retrograde P after a PVC signals VA conduction that resets the sinus node, explaining a longer, non-compensatory pause.
items.a: [blog] PVCs With VA Conduction

items.c: RBBB gives an upright terminal deflection in V1-V2 with wide terminal S waves in the leftward leads I, aVL, V5-V6.
items.a: [blog] Right Bundle Branch Block

items.t: [blog] Second-degree AV Block with Left Bundle Branch Block & Lead Reversal
items.c: Mobitz II with a bundle branch block often represents intermittent trifascicular block, and complete block occurs when all fascicles fail simultaneously.
items.a: [blog] Second-degree AV Block with Left Bundle Branch Block & Lead Reversal
items.rn: [blog] Second-degree AV Block with Left Bundle Branch Block & Lead Reversal

items.t: [blog] Second-degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II
items.c: A 2:1 AV block cannot be classified as Mobitz I or II from the ratio alone; label it high-grade until other strips clarify the mechanism.
items.a: [blog] Second-degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II
items.rn: [blog] Second-degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II

items.t: [blog] Second degree AVB Mobitz Type II
items.c: To confirm Mobitz II, compare the PR interval just before and just after the dropped beat; they must be equal.

In pathology, there is no truth in names; cystic medial necrosis may lack necrosis and not be cystic. The characteristic features are: Basophilic ground substance in the media (seen on Movat's stain). Disruption of the elastic lamina (seen with an elastic stain). +/-Focal necrosis.
